sections.html: Bureau County is a mostly rural county in north-central Illinois. Princeton is the biggest city and holds the courthouse. The county estimate for 2025 is 32,510 residents, and the county has 15,663 housing units with a 76.1% ownership rate. The median owned home is worth $126,900, so most sales here sit well below suburban Chicago prices. A buyer's inspector will likely look hard at the basement and roof, so fix obvious problems before you set a price.

Two offices of the county sit in the courthouse at 700 South Main Street in Princeton, open weekdays from eight to four. The treasurer, who doubles as county collector, prepares and collects the bills. The Supervisor of Assessments supports the township assessors, processes exemptions, and acts as clerk to the Board of Review.

Each township has an elected assessor who finds and values property first, before the county reviews anything. If a bill arrives for a house you no longer own, tell the treasurer so it can be sent back promptly.

Bureau County mails a single bill that you can pay in two installments, and it will not take a partial payment on either one. The state statute counts an installment as late after the later of June 1 or the day following the date shown on the bill (35 ILCS 200/21-15), so the coupon on your own bill is the date that counts. A bill that never shows up, or shows up late, does not wipe out the tax or the late charge.

  • In the office, pay by check or cash. Make checks payable to "Bureau County Collector."
  • By mail, send payment to Bureau County Collector, 700 S. Main St., Room 103, Princeton, IL 61356. A postmark on the due date is acceptable.
  • Online, pay by debit card, credit card or e-check through Illinois ePAY. This works only through the second installment due date.
  • If a mortgage company pays your bill, check with that company yourself that the payment went out.

Your canceled check works as the receipt. If you want a separate one, include a stamped, self-addressed envelope with your payment.

Three charges can stack up. Past the due date, interest accrues at 1.5% per installment per month, and the coupons print the late-payment schedule. A payment sent without the late fees comes back to you. A further $10.00 is added to any tax still unpaid after the second installment date, which covers publication and the certified delinquent notice.

After those notices are mailed, the collector takes only certified funds: a cashier's check, money order or cash. Personal and business checks are refused. At the end of each tax year the collector holds a sale of the tax on every parcel still unpaid.

If you have fallen behind, clear the balance before you list. An open delinquency shows up in the title search and can stall a closing. Call the treasurer at 815-872-3241 for the payoff on each installment, and ask for certified-funds instructions if delinquent notices have already been mailed.

A cash buyer can close faster than a buyer who needs a lender, which helps when you want the back taxes settled out of the sale proceeds on a short timeline. The title company will deduct what is owed at closing, so having the figure early avoids surprises on the settlement statement.

A practical order of steps: get the payoff from the treasurer, confirm which installments are open, pay certified funds if notices have gone out, and ask for a written receipt to hand the title company.

The standard for nonfarm property in Illinois is 33 1/3% of fair market value, and Bureau County's Board of Review rules apply it too. If you disagree with your value, file an appeal form with the Board's clerk, the Supervisor of Assessments, by the thirtieth day after your township's assessment list is published. Filing costs nothing. You need a separate form for each parcel unless the parcels are contiguous and similarly classified.

Complaints must be about market value or equity. A tax bill that simply feels too big is not a valid complaint. For a home, the Board looks for:

  • Proof of a recent sale or purchase of the property.
  • A recent appraisal from an Illinois certified appraiser, delivered within 30 calendar days after the filing deadline and prepared to professional standards.
  • At least three recent sales of comparable properties, or assessed values of comparables if equity is the issue.
  • Dated photographs if you claim a condition problem.

The Board sends a tentative notice, and an owner who is unhappy with it has ten days to schedule a hearing. Each hearing gets a 15-minute slot in the Supervisor of Assessments' office. Speak for yourself or send an Illinois attorney, but do not skip it, because a missed hearing can end in dismissal. An incomplete form is returned once, with ten more calendar days to fix it.

Homestead exemptions are applied under state statute and Department of Revenue guidelines. Any application is due by December 31. The Supervisor of Assessments processes exemption, preferential assessment and abatement applications and applies them to eligible parcels.

Exemptions depend on who owns and lives in the home, so a buyer should expect to apply in their own name. As a seller, ask the Supervisor of Assessments which exemptions sit on your parcel and bring that list to the closing so credits are figured on real numbers. The county website carries the Board's rules and the appeal form, plus GIS imagery that shows parcel boundaries and aerial photos.

Because Illinois bills a year in arrears, the first bill after a sale usually covers time the seller owned the house. Many contracts deal with that through a seller credit at closing for tax not yet billed, and yours can spell it out. For the payment status of the parcel, call the treasurer's office at 815-872-3241.

  • Confirm whether both installments of the prior bill are paid.
  • Agree in the contract how the next bill will be split.
  • Give the county the buyer's mailing address so assessment notices and bills reach the right person.
  • Keep copies of the deed and transfer paperwork. The Board of Review accepts a recent purchase as evidence of value.
  • Bring a photo ID and the parcel number if you visit the treasurer's counter for a payoff figure.

faqs.q: How many installments does Bureau County property tax have?
faqs.a: Two. One bill arrives and is payable in two installments, and the county refuses partial payments. The coupon on your bill shows each date.

faqs.q: Is there a fee to appeal a Bureau County assessment?
faqs.a: No. Filing an appeal with the Board of Review costs nothing. The deadline is the thirtieth day after your township's assessment list is published.

faqs.q: Can I pay Bureau County tax with a credit card?
faqs.a: Yes, online through Illinois ePAY by debit card, credit card or e-check, until the second installment due date. The treasurer's counter takes only checks and cash.

faqs.q: What happens to Bureau County tax I do not pay?
faqs.a: Interest builds at 1.5% per installment per month, $10.00 is added after the second installment date, and the collector holds a tax sale on unpaid parcels at year end. After notices go out, only certified funds are taken.

faqs.q: Where do I file a homestead exemption in Bureau County?
faqs.a: With the Supervisor of Assessments, 700 South Main Street, Suite 12, Princeton, phone 815-875-6478. December 31 is the deadline to apply.
